questions.prompt: This is the start of the DPLL pseudocode. Fill in the value that is returned. Type it exactly as the pseudocode writes it.
questions.explain: When no clauses are left, every clause has been satisfied, so the formula is satisfiable and DPLL returns `True`. The trap is to mix this up with the next test: when F contains the **empty clause**, a clause that lost all its literals, DPLL returns `False`.

questions.prompt: DPLL by hand uses this order: unit clause, then pure literal, then split (first variable in the alphabet, False before True). What is the first step on this clause set?
options: Pure literal: assign True to Q
Unit clause: assign True to Q
questions.explain: There is no unit clause, because every clause has two literals. `Q` occurs three times and `¬Q` never, so Q is a pure literal and is made true before any split. The trap is to split on P straight away. P and R occur with both signs, so they are not pure.

questions.prompt: Assign the value False to P in this clause set. Which clause set is the result?
questions.explain: P = False makes the literal `¬P` true. The clause `¬P∨R` contains it and is removed. The clauses `P∨Q` and `P∨¬Q∨S` contain the opposite literal P, so they are shortened to `Q` and `¬Q∨S`. The trap is the mirror image `{ R, ¬R∨S }`, which is what P = True gives.

questions.prompt: This DPLL trace ends with no clauses left. Type the model in the format `P=True,Q=True,R=True`, with your own values and without spaces.
questions.explain: The model is read from the successful branch only: P = True after the backtrack, then R = False and Q = False from the unit clauses `¬R` and `¬Q`. The trap is to take R = True from the first branch. That branch ended in a contradiction, so its values are thrown away.
